questions.question: Does putting a mutable request object onto a BlockingQueue make it safe to keep changing that object?
questions.answer: No. The queue provides a safe handoff for actions before insertion to the consumer accessing that element. It does not take ownership of all later mutations or copy the object graph. If the producer changes a list inside the request after enqueueing, the consumer can race with it. I prefer immutable task inputs with defensive copies of mutable members, or an explicit ownership transfer where the producer stops touching the object. A final field only fixes the reference; a record containing a mutable list is not automatically deeply immutable. For large payloads, copying everything may be costly, so ownership can be the better design, but the rule must hold on success, retry and cancellation paths.

followups.q: Is an unmodifiable view a defensive snapshot?
followups.a: Not if its mutable backing collection can still change. A view prevents mutation through that view, not through other references.

followups.q: Does List.copyOf deeply copy elements?
followups.a: No. It creates an unmodifiable list but mutable element objects still need their own ownership or immutability rule.

followups.q: Can two retries share the same mutable task input?
followups.a: Only if their accesses are coordinated. Immutable inputs avoid accidental cross-attempt mutation.

questions.trap: Assuming a thread-safe queue makes every object stored in it thread-safe.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Distinct from publication: this tests mutation after ownership handoff. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: A synchronized method prevents duplicate processing locally, but duplicates appear after scaling to two pods. Why?
questions.answer: A monitor belongs to an object in one JVM. The other pod has different memory and a different monitor, so neither excludes the other. I would move the duplicate-processing invariant to a shared authority, often a unique database constraint on an idempotency key plus an atomic transaction that records the business outcome. A distributed lease can coordinate work but is not automatically a correctness guarantee: an old owner can continue after its lease expires. Fencing can help when the protected resource rejects stale owners. For external side effects, such as a remote API call, the local database transaction cannot roll that call back, so the remote API's idempotency contract or a durable workflow matters too.

followups.q: Does a static synchronized method coordinate all pods?
followups.a: No. Its Class monitor is still local to that JVM and class definition.

followups.q: Why not check for a row and then insert?
followups.a: Two pods can both pass the check. The database must enforce the invariant atomically, such as through a unique constraint.

followups.q: Does recording a key always mean the work succeeded?
followups.a: No. Define pending, completed and failed states, and how retries discover or resume an uncertain outcome.

questions.trap: Using a distributed lock as a substitute for defining durable idempotency and external-side-effect semantics.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Focus is the scope of synchronization; distributed design detail belongs in S08/S13. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Future.cancel(true) returns true, but a CPU-heavy worker keeps running. How would you fix the task?
questions.answer: Cancellation of a FutureTask can record a cancelled outcome and request interruption, but it cannot safely inject a stop into arbitrary computation. A tight loop that never checks interruption can keep consuming CPU after callers see CancellationException. I would check isInterrupted at meaningful chunk boundaries, then exit through cleanup before publishing a final result. The check frequency trades responsiveness against overhead, so I set a cancellation-latency target. Partial output must have a defined status; cancellation should not expose a half-built result as success. I also inspect library calls inside each chunk because an unresponsive native or blocking operation can dominate cancellation latency even when the outer loop is cooperative.

followups.q: Does isDone prove computation has stopped?
followups.a: No. A cancelled future is done from the Future contract's perspective even if its underlying task ignores interruption.

followups.q: Why not use Thread.stop?
followups.a: It is not a safe supported cancellation design; forced termination can violate invariants and bypass application-level recovery.

followups.q: How do you verify the worker really exited?
followups.a: Observe a task-owned completion signal or executor termination with a bounded wait, not only the future's cancelled state.

questions.trap: Interpreting successful future cancellation as proof that the underlying computation has already stopped.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Applies interruption mechanics to CPU loops and Future completion semantics. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: How would you choose concurrency limits for a connector that fans out to a database and a rate-limited API?
questions.answer: I would budget each constrained resource separately: database connections, simultaneous API requests, permitted requests per time window, and buffered tasks. A bigger executor does not create more database capacity or relax a remote rate limit. As an initial estimate, average in-flight work is throughput multiplied by average time in the system under stable conditions, but I would measure tail latency and bursts before selecting limits. Fan-out multiplies downstream demand, and retries consume the same budget as original attempts. I would bound admission, use per-dependency concurrency control and a rate limiter where required, and monitor queue age as well as depth. The final settings come from measured workload and dependency contracts, not from numbers invented for my resume.

followups.q: Does the resume's integrations-per-hour figure determine pool size?
followups.a: No. It lacks task duration, fan-out, peak distribution and downstream limits, so it is insufficient for sizing.

followups.q: Should retries bypass admission to finish sooner?
followups.a: No. That can amplify an outage. Include retries in the same resource budgets and use bounded attempts with backoff.

followups.q: Why monitor queue age?
followups.a: A queue can remain below capacity while its oldest tasks have already exceeded their useful deadline.

questions.trap: Choosing a pool from CPU count alone for an I/O workflow, or confusing a requests-per-second quota with a concurrent-request limit.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed design. No unsupported connector internals, ownership claims or sizing measurements are asserted. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Is a singleton Spring service thread-safe if all of its dependencies are injected correctly?
questions.answer: Singleton scope controls how many bean instances the container manages, not how many threads can enter their methods. Concurrent requests can execute the same service instance. I would keep request-specific values in parameters and local variables instead of fields such as currentTenant or lastRequest. A local reference is not sufficient if it points to a shared mutable object, so I also inspect the dependencies and object graph. Immutable configuration and stateless operations are straightforward; shared counters, caches and mutable formatters need their own concurrency contracts. Adding synchronized to every service method would serialize unrelated requests and would not protect other beans accessing the same state. Injection alone is not a thread-safety mechanism.

followups.q: Does prototype scope automatically fix this?
followups.a: No. A prototype injected once into a singleton is normally that same dependency for subsequent calls, and external shared state remains shared.

followups.q: Are method-local variables always safe?
followups.a: The local variable belongs to the invocation, but the object it references may still be shared and mutable.

questions.trap: Equating one managed instance with one request at a time, or placing the current user's state in singleton fields.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Frequency, round and level are estimates; no company attribution.

questions.question: An idle worker consumes an entire core while repeatedly checking whether a queue has work. What would you change?
questions.answer: The worker is busy-waiting: it repeatedly polls without giving up execution capacity when there is nothing useful to do. I would normally use a BlockingQueue take, or a timed poll when the worker has another deadline to check. That parks the worker until work, interruption or timeout rather than burning a core. Sleeping in the loop reduces CPU usage but trades it for polling latency and does not provide a proper notification protocol. Thread.onSpinWait is a processor hint, not a visibility guarantee or a blocking operation. Deliberate spinning can suit specialized short waits, but an integration worker waiting for sporadic work should normally use blocking coordination and respond to cancellation.

followups.q: Does Thread.yield guarantee another worker runs?
followups.a: No. It is a scheduling hint and cannot establish fairness, ordering or a happens-before relationship.

followups.q: What evidence identifies this problem?
followups.a: High per-thread CPU and repeated stack samples in the polling loop while useful throughput is low.

questions.trap: Adding onSpinWait and assuming the queue check is now blocking or correctly synchronized.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Distinct from low-CPU waiting diagnosis in 044. Round, level and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Why can submit return a Future that never completes when a saturated pool uses DiscardPolicy?
questions.answer: In a standard ThreadPoolExecutor, submit creates a task wrapper representing a future and passes it to execute. DiscardPolicy silently returns when the pool rejects the task. The wrapper was never run and was not cancelled, so submit can return a future with no path to completion. A caller waiting without a timeout can hang forever. DiscardOldestPolicy can similarly strand the future of an evicted queued task. I would prefer explicit rejection that reaches the submitter, or a carefully defined handler that cancels discarded future tasks and reports loss. Every accepted task handle needs a terminal outcome; having a Future object is not evidence that the executor accepted its work.

followups.q: Can CallerRunsPolicy also discard?
followups.a: Yes. Its standard implementation does not run the rejected task once the executor is shut down, which can leave a submitted wrapper unresolved.

followups.q: Does a timeout on get fix the executor's lifecycle?
followups.a: It bounds the caller's wait but does not itself complete or cancel the abandoned task wrapper.

questions.trap: Assuming every rejection policy either executes the task or completes its future exceptionally.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests future lifecycle rather than the policy definitions in 016. Round, level and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: A request has a one-second budget but performs three waits. How do you prevent each wait from consuming a fresh second?
questions.answer: I establish one deadline for the operation and pass the remaining budget into each blocking step, including admission, connection acquisition and result waiting. Before starting another step I subtract elapsed time and fail promptly if no budget remains. For elapsed time within one JVM I use System.nanoTime differences rather than wall-clock timestamps, which can jump after clock adjustments. Its arbitrary origin means I cannot transmit a nanoTime value to another machine as a shared deadline. I also reserve time for response assembly and cleanup instead of using the entire budget downstream. This limits how long the caller waits; it still requires explicit transport timeouts and cancellation policies to bound underlying resource use.

followups.q: Does queueing time count?
followups.a: Yes. Starting the timeout only when a worker begins ignores time already spent waiting for admission or execution.

followups.q: Can retries reset the deadline?
followups.a: Not for the same request budget. Each retry consumes remaining time and must still leave room for completion or recovery.

questions.trap: Applying the full original timeout independently to each sequential stage and calling it an end-to-end limit.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Focus is local deadline measurement, not timeout-versus-cancellation semantics in 027. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: When would you choose ExecutorService.invokeAll or invokeAny, and how is invokeAny different from CompletableFuture.anyOf?
questions.answer: invokeAll waits for the submitted set and returns futures in input order, so I still inspect each future for success or failure. Its timed overload cancels unfinished tasks when the timeout expires. invokeAny seeks one successfully completed result and cancels unfinished tasks when it returns or throws; a single early failure need not end the search while another task can succeed. CompletableFuture.anyOf instead completes on the first completion, even an exceptional one, and does not automatically cancel the other computations. I choose based on the outcome contract, not similar names. Cancellation is still cooperative, and returning the winning result does not prove every losing task has already stopped consuming resources.

followups.q: Does invokeAll throw each task's exception directly?
followups.a: Task failures are represented by their returned futures. The coordinator must read them; invocation-level interruption and submission failure are separate.

followups.q: Is invokeAny suitable for redundant writes?
followups.a: Only with deliberately defined side-effect and idempotency semantics; losing requests may already have changed remote state.

questions.trap: Treating invokeAny as simply another spelling of first-completion anyOf.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Frequency, round and level are estimates; no company attribution.

questions.question: For a bounded producer-consumer buffer, how would you choose between ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue?
questions.answer: I would start with a capacity derived from memory and latency budgets, then compare the workload. ArrayBlockingQueue stores references in a fixed array and uses one lock with separate conditions for producers and consumers; it avoids allocating a linked node for each insertion. LinkedBlockingQueue uses linked nodes and separate put and take locks, allowing more producer-consumer overlap in suitable workloads, but it adds allocation and memory overhead. I would explicitly set its capacity because its default bound is effectively enormous. Neither implementation is universally faster, and the queue's capacity counts elements, not payload bytes. Large or variable-sized records may need an additional byte budget to prevent a numerically small backlog from exhausting memory.

followups.q: Does an array queue preallocate every payload?
followups.a: No. It reserves reference slots; the objects referenced by those slots consume separate memory.

followups.q: What should a performance comparison measure?
followups.a: The actual producer/consumer ratio, payload lifetime, allocation rate, throughput and waiting latency with equivalent capacity and correctness requirements.

questions.trap: Calling a bounded element count a strict memory bound without accounting for payload sizes.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests queue representation and memory budgeting beyond the producer-consumer protocol in 008. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Your afterExecute hook receives a null Throwable even though a submitted task failed. How should the hook inspect the outcome?
questions.answer: The hook's Throwable argument describes an exception that escaped task execution. FutureTask captures its computation's failure, so the wrapper returns normally and that argument can be null. For a completed runnable that is also a Future, the hook can inspect get, distinguish cancellation, and unwrap ExecutionException to report the cause. I check isDone before reading so instrumentation cannot block a worker on an incomplete future, which matters for reusable periodic futures. Interruption during inspection needs proper propagation or restoration. The reporting path itself must be bounded and must not throw into the executor; a telemetry failure should not kill workers. This catches failures but does not replace the business caller's responsibility to handle its result.

followups.q: Why not call get on every RunnableFuture?
followups.a: A periodic scheduled future can remain incomplete between successful runs, so unconditional get can park the worker indefinitely.

followups.q: Should every cancellation be logged as an error?
followups.a: No. Distinguish expected cancellation from unexpected task failure, and preserve appropriate metrics for both.

questions.trap: Treating a null hook Throwable as proof of business success, or making the diagnostic hook block on a recurring future.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. GAP follows the explicitly supplied ThreadPoolExecutor failure-handling gap; this tests the hook implementation contract rather than the explanation in 017.

questions.question: Can a whenComplete callback turn a successful CompletableFuture chain into a failure?
questions.answer: Yes. whenComplete returns a dependent stage; it does not mutate the already completed source. If the source succeeds and the observer throws, that returned stage completes exceptionally with the observer's failure. If the source already failed and the observer also throws, the source failure takes precedence for the dependent outcome. So calling it observation-only describes its intended use, not a guarantee that arbitrary observer code cannot change the downstream result. I would keep logging or metrics callbacks small and handle expected telemetry failures deliberately. I also ensure the returned stage is observed, because ignoring it can hide an observer failure even while the source's result looks successful.

followups.q: Would handle behave the same way?
followups.a: No. handle deliberately maps either outcome to a new result, though its callback can also throw and fail its dependent stage.

followups.q: Which future should a caller return after adding the observer?
followups.a: Choose intentionally: returning the dependent stage exposes observer failure, while returning the source does not represent that observer's completion.

questions.trap: Claiming whenComplete cannot affect downstream success because it cannot return a replacement value.

code.output:
source result: ok
dependent failure: observer failed
failed source cause: original failed
failed dependent cause: original failed
All assertions passed.

questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Narrows the observer exception edge case beyond basic error handlers in 021. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: If supplyAsync uses your custom executor, will later thenApplyAsync stages automatically use that same executor?
questions.answer: Not for an ordinary CompletableFuture. Passing an executor to supplyAsync chooses where that supplier runs; it does not permanently bind the whole chain to that executor. Async continuations without an explicit executor use the stage's default asynchronous facility, normally the common pool for ordinary CompletableFuture instances. Non-async continuations may run on a completing thread or an attaching caller if the predecessor is already complete. I would pass the intended executor at important async boundaries and keep non-async callbacks short. Otherwise a blocking transform can unexpectedly occupy a shared pool or a completion thread used by an HTTP client. Executor placement is part of the chain's resource design, not just a naming convention.

followups.q: Does an Async suffix guarantee a different physical thread?
followups.a: No. The executor controls execution; a direct executor or a caller-runs policy can execute on the submitting thread.

followups.q: Can a CompletableFuture subclass customize the default?
followups.a: Yes, but that is a deliberate subclass contract. Do not infer it from supplying a custom executor to one factory call.

questions.trap: Assuming a custom executor passed at the start is inherited by every asynchronous continuation.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern for ordinary Java 21 CompletableFuture instances. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: In Java 21, why can returning a future from inside a try-with-resources ExecutorService block still block the caller?
questions.answer: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable in Java 21, and its close waits for termination after initiating shutdown. Before a method can finish returning from the try block, try-with-resources invokes close. If the submitted computation is still running, the return is therefore delayed even though the return type is a future. This can be exactly right for a bounded operation that owns all its tasks, but wrong for an API meant to return immediately. In the latter case I would use an executor owned by a longer-lived component with an explicit shutdown lifecycle. Ownership also prevents a request from closing a shared application executor. A blocking close has no application-specific deadline built into the try-with-resources syntax.

followups.q: Does shutdown have the same waiting behavior?
followups.a: No. shutdown initiates orderly shutdown without waiting; close adds a termination wait.

followups.q: What if tasks never finish?
followups.a: Close can wait indefinitely. Task cancellation, I/O timeouts and a bounded shutdown strategy must be designed separately.

questions.trap: Equating an asynchronous return type with a nonblocking method regardless of resource cleanup at the return boundary.
questions.notes: Unverified interview pattern. API assumptions are Java 21; no company attribution. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Why might a ThreadLocal cache become expensive after moving from a fixed pool to virtual-thread-per-task execution?
questions.answer: A ThreadLocal value belongs to the virtual thread, not its carrier. In a small fixed pool, caching an expensive object per worker bounds the number of cached instances roughly by worker count. With many live virtual threads, that same pattern can create many expensive objects at once and lose the reuse the original cache relied on. Virtual threads reduce the cost of representing blocked work, not the cost of everything stored in each task. I would inspect allocation profiles and retained objects, share immutable helpers where appropriate, and use an explicit bounded pool for genuinely scarce resources. Per-request context can still belong in thread-local state, but heavyweight resource caching should not scale accidentally with request concurrency.

followups.q: Does a carrier reuse the virtual thread's ThreadLocal values?
followups.a: No. They are associated with the virtual thread, so carrier reuse does not provide the old worker-local cache reuse.

followups.q: Should you pool virtual threads to fix this?
followups.a: Usually not. Bound the scarce resource itself and eliminate unnecessary per-thread heavyweight state.

questions.trap: Assuming cheap virtual threads make a large per-thread cache cheap too.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests migration allocation costs rather than the stale pooled-thread leak in 023. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: After cancelling many queued tasks, why can a thread pool still retain their wrappers and report a large queue?
questions.answer: Cancellation changes the future's state; it does not universally remove its wrapper from the executor's queue at that instant. A ThreadPoolExecutor may retain cancelled queued wrappers until workers take them or cleanup removes them. The wrapper and remaining references can consume memory and queue slots, even though cancellation may clear some task references. ThreadPoolExecutor provides purge for cancelled futures, and explicit removal is possible when the queued object is known. ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor has a remove-on-cancel policy that can avoid retaining cancelled delayed tasks until their delays expire. I would confirm the actual queue and retained graph before tuning cleanup, because cancelled wrapper retention is different from an underlying operation that ignores cancellation and keeps running.

followups.q: Can you remove the original Runnable after submit?
followups.a: Not necessarily. The queue usually contains a wrapper created by submit, not the original Runnable reference.

followups.q: Should purge run on every request?
followups.a: Not automatically. It has traversal cost; measure the retention problem and select an appropriate cleanup or executor policy.

questions.trap: Assuming isCancelled proves the task wrapper is no longer queued or reachable.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Distinct from stopping a running CPU task in 049. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Why can sleeping inside executor tasks during retry backoff cause a service to stop making progress?
questions.answer: In a bounded platform-thread pool, sleeping tasks keep their worker slots throughout the backoff. During a downstream outage, enough sleeping retries can occupy the entire pool and prevent unrelated useful work from running. I would schedule the next attempt without holding a worker during the delay, then re-enter normal admission when it becomes due. The timer callback should be short, not execute a blocking remote call itself. Scheduling is not a free capacity solution: a delayed-task queue can accumulate an enormous number of retries unless attempts, queued retry count and total deadline are bounded. I would also add jitter to avoid synchronized retry bursts and ensure rejected resubmissions terminate their caller-visible outcomes.

followups.q: Do virtual threads remove every cost of waiting?
followups.a: No. Parking may release the carrier, but waiting tasks still retain state and any application permits or resources they hold.

followups.q: Should a downstream concurrency permit be held through backoff?
followups.a: Usually a permit representing an active request should be released between attempts. Define separate admission limits for outstanding logical operations.

questions.trap: Moving sleeps into an unbounded delayed queue and declaring overload solved.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed scheduling design. No claim about Harsh's actual Resilience4j configuration. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: How can a poison-pill shutdown lose work if producers are still active?
questions.answer: A poison pill is a message in the queue, not a global signal that no more work exists. If a producer appends real work after it, a consumer can exit first and leave that work stranded. For graceful shutdown I stop admission, wait for active producers to finish publishing, then insert termination markers according to the consumer protocol and wait for consumers to finish processing. Bounded queues complicate marker insertion because shutdown itself can block when the buffer is full. I need a deadline and a fallback policy for draining, persistence or cancellation. For multiple stages, I preserve the same upstream-before-downstream ordering rather than shutting every executor simultaneously.

followups.q: How many markers are needed?
followups.a: For the simple one-marker-per-consumer design, one per consumer after all producers finish. Other protocols need an explicit, tested propagation rule.

followups.q: Does an empty queue prove the pipeline is idle?
followups.a: No. Consumers may still be processing dequeued work, or producers may be about to publish more.

questions.trap: Checking queue emptiness once or inserting a marker while live producers can still enqueue behind it.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests multistage drain ordering beyond executor shutdown methods in 018. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: What does it mean for a concurrent operation to be linearizable, and why is passing a throughput test insufficient?
questions.answer: Linearizability means each operation can be viewed as taking effect at one instant between its invocation and return, while preserving real-time order for operations that do not overlap. For example, an atomic conditional reservation should have one decisive point at which capacity is either consumed or refused. Individual atomic reads and writes do not automatically make a larger check-then-act method linearizable. A throughput test measures how much work completes, not whether observed outcomes admit a legal sequential explanation. I would define the object's contract, identify the proposed atomic decision point, and test histories against allowed outcomes. Some useful aggregates deliberately offer weaker semantics, but then callers must not use them as exact admission decisions.

followups.q: Does overlapping execution violate linearizability?
followups.a: No. Operations may overlap physically as long as their observed outcomes can be ordered according to the contract.

followups.q: Does linearizability guarantee fairness?
followups.a: No. It is a safety property; progress, starvation and response-time guarantees are separate.

questions.trap: Treating high throughput or absence of exceptions as proof that concurrent outcomes are correct.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. A correctness-contract question, not another implementation of the multi-field update in 030. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: How do you safely use a StampedLock optimistic read for two related scalar fields?
questions.answer: I obtain an optimistic stamp, copy both fields into local variables, and validate the stamp after those reads. If validation succeeds, the copied pair can be used according to the lock's guarantees. If it fails or the initial stamp is invalid, I acquire the read lock, read both fields again and release that lock in finally. I must not read the shared fields again after successful validation and assume those new reads are protected. This works best for short, side-effect-free reads of simple state. Traversing an actively mutated object graph before validation can already throw or produce invalid intermediate behavior, so validation is not a general excuse to read arbitrary mutable structures without protection.

followups.q: Does an optimistic stamp prevent a writer?
followups.a: No. It is not a held read lock; a writer can proceed and make validation fail.

followups.q: Why not call a callback before validation?
followups.a: The callback may act on inconsistent data or cause irreversible side effects before you discover that the optimistic read failed.

questions.trap: Validating first and then reading, or repeating reads from shared state after validation instead of using the validated local copy.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests the validation protocol and side-effect boundary beyond the comparison in 012. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: One tenant fills a shared executor's queue. How can you protect other tenants without creating one thread pool per tenant?
questions.answer: I would separate admission from worker allocation. A global bound protects the process, while per-tenant outstanding-work limits prevent one tenant from reserving every queue slot. A bounded dispatcher can then choose ready work across tenants, using a simple round-robin or weighted policy when different service tiers require it. Workers remain shared, so the number of tenants does not determine the number of OS threads. The dispatcher must also limit active tenant bookkeeping and clean up idle entries safely. A fair lock alone does not provide tenant fairness because it orders lock contenders, not each tenant's queued work or execution cost. I would measure per-tenant queue age and completions to validate the policy.

followups.q: Is equal task count always fair?
followups.a: No. Tasks can differ greatly in cost; the policy may need cost estimates or separate limits for scarce dependencies.

followups.q: Can a tenant release someone else's admission slot?
followups.a: The implementation must associate release with the admitted task and tenant, including failure and cancellation paths.

questions.trap: Calling a global FIFO queue tenant-fair when one tenant can place thousands of tasks ahead of every other tenant.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed design. This tests fairness across tenants rather than record ordering within a key in 045. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Several workers append records to one export file. How do you prevent interleaved records and detect write failure?
questions.answer: I would give one writer ownership of the file and hand it complete records through a bounded queue. That makes the record boundary explicit and gives producers backpressure. Alternatively, every writer in the same process can use one shared lock around the entire logical record, but locking individual character writes is not enough. I would not assume append mode makes arbitrary multi-call record writes atomic across threads or processes. Writer failure needs a shared failure signal so producers stop or fail instead of waiting forever on a full queue. Completion means all accepted records were processed and the writer was closed successfully; flushing buffers alone is not a universal guarantee of durable storage after a machine crash.

followups.q: How would you preserve input order?
followups.a: Assign sequence numbers before parallel processing and explicitly reorder at the writer, with a bound on the reordering buffer.

followups.q: Does a Java lock coordinate a second process?
followups.a: No. Cross-process file ownership or locking is a different protocol, with filesystem-specific behavior to verify.

questions.trap: Assuming append mode or individually synchronized writes preserve the boundaries of a record assembled through multiple calls.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed export design, not a claim about Harsh's connector internals. No filesystem-specific atomicity guarantee is asserted.

questions.question: You atomically replace a shared HTTP client during configuration refresh. Is it safe to immediately close the old client?
questions.answer: Atomic replacement safely changes which reference new readers obtain, but existing requests may still hold the old client. Closing it immediately can interrupt those requests, depending on the client's close contract. Publication and reclamation are separate problems. I would give requests a lease on a client generation, retire the old generation so no new lease can begin, and close it after its active leases drain or an explicit shutdown deadline is reached. The lease acquisition and retirement protocol itself must be atomic with respect to each other; reading a reference and incrementing a counter later can race with closure. A mature client or resource manager may already provide graceful draining, which is preferable to inventing an unsafe protocol.

followups.q: Why does garbage collection not solve this?
followups.a: Reachability is not a graceful-close protocol for external connections and resources; explicit closure can affect users that still hold a reference.

followups.q: Can a failed refresh close the current client?
followups.a: It should not accidentally do so. Construct and validate the candidate before publication, and separately clean up unsuccessful candidates.

questions.trap: Treating visibility-safe reference replacement as proof that no thread is still using the replaced resource.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed lifecycle design. Exact close behavior depends on the chosen client; no library-specific behavior is assumed.

questions.question: Why is invoking a plugin callback while holding an internal lock dangerous even if the lock is reentrant?
questions.answer: Reentrancy only allows the same thread to acquire the same lock again. A callback can block on I/O, acquire another lock in a conflicting order, or re-enter an operation while my internal state is only partly updated. I would normally finish the invariant-preserving update under the lock, capture the immutable notification data, release the lock, and invoke callbacks afterward. That changes the timing contract: another update can occur before the callback runs, so the notification should describe a particular version rather than imply it is the latest state. If strict notification order is required, I would use a serialized dispatcher instead of keeping arbitrary plugin code inside the critical section.

followups.q: Can moving callbacks outside the lock introduce races?
followups.a: Yes, if they rely on live mutable state. Capture the required data and define ordering or version semantics explicitly.

followups.q: Should callback failure roll back the internal update?
followups.a: That is a business contract, not an automatic lock behavior. Usually notifications and committed state need explicit failure and retry semantics.

questions.trap: Assuming reentrant means safe to call arbitrary code while internal invariants are temporarily broken.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests reentrancy and callback contracts rather than a repeat of lock-order deadlock avoidance. Round and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: A CountDownLatch reaches zero after workers decrement it in finally. Does that mean the batch succeeded?
questions.answer: No. The latch tracks arrivals, not business outcomes. Decrementing in finally ensures a failing worker does not strand the coordinator, but it deliberately makes success and failure both count as completion. Each worker must publish an explicit result, or the coordinator must inspect its future after the latch releases. CountDownLatch's visibility guarantee makes actions before countDown visible after a successful await, but it does not make conflicting writes to the same result container safe while workers are running. Separate result slots or a suitable concurrent collection avoid that race. The coordinator then applies the batch policy: all-success, partial success, retry or compensation, rather than declaring success because waiting ended.

followups.q: Can a timed await returning false inspect a complete batch?
followups.a: No. It reports that the count did not reach zero within the wait; incomplete results still need an explicit handling policy.

followups.q: What if task submission fails before a worker runs?
followups.a: Record that failure and reconcile the latch accounting; there will be no worker finally block to decrement for that task.

questions.trap: Using a synchronization signal as the success signal, or expecting its visibility guarantee to serialize concurrent writes before completion.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Focus is completion signaling and result publication, distinct from Phaser registration in 046.

questions.question: How do you reliably verify that an asynchronous operation sends exactly one notification, including the possibility of a late duplicate?
questions.answer: Waiting until one notification appears proves only that at least one has arrived so far. To assert exactly one, I need a completion boundary after which this operation cannot send another. Ideally the API returns a future that completes after all its owned work and callbacks finish; the test waits with a timeout, then checks the final count and surfaces every task failure. If retry or delayed work can outlive that future, the contract is incomplete for this assertion. I would inject a controllable executor or scheduler where appropriate and drive all relevant work to completion. Arbitrary sleeps and a timeout-based mock verification alone do not establish that a late duplicate is impossible.

followups.q: Should the test shut down a shared application executor?
followups.a: No. Test ownership must be explicit; clean up only resources created and owned by that test.

followups.q: Can a fake executor hide bugs?
followups.a: Yes. Synchronous execution can hide races or thread-local differences, so retain focused real-executor integration tests for those contracts.

questions.trap: Equating 'the first call arrived before the timeout' with 'the operation can never call again'.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Tests final outcome assertions, not forced interleavings or JMM stress behavior from 042.

questions.question: A user-triggered operation is moved to a background executor. Which identity should authorize its work?
questions.answer: Moving threads does not define the authorization contract. I first decide whether the task is delegated user work or a service-owned job. For short in-process delegated work, a supported security-context executor wrapper can establish and restore the intended context on the worker, but copying context does not refresh credentials or solve revocation. For delayed or durable work, I would persist only the permitted identity and authorization metadata, not blindly serialize thread-local state or long-lived bearer tokens. At execution time the service must enforce the chosen tenant and permission rules. Retrying a job under a more privileged service account can accidentally expand its authority, so that policy must be explicit and auditable.

followups.q: Does propagating MDC authorize the worker?
followups.a: No. Logging labels are not a trusted security context or proof of permission.

followups.q: Is reusing the original Authentication object always safe?
followups.a: No. Consider mutability, lifetime and the framework's supported propagation contract; do not share changing authentication state casually.

questions.trap: Solving a lost ThreadLocal by granting every background task a privileged service identity without defining delegated authority.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed authorization design. Distinct from logging-context restoration in 039; exact security-wrapper configuration is not asserted.

questions.question: If logging is asynchronous, can it still cause request latency or memory problems?
questions.answer: Yes. Asynchronous logging transfers work through a buffer; it does not remove the sink's throughput limit. When the sink slows, an unbounded buffer can retain large event payloads, while a bounded one must block producers, drop events or apply another explicit overflow policy. Blocking can feed latency back into request threads, especially if logging happens while they hold application locks. I would inspect the actual logger's configured overflow and shutdown behavior, monitor queue pressure and dropped-event counts, and distinguish best-effort diagnostics from required audit records. Formatting or copying context can also cost time before enqueueing. Calling a logger async therefore says little about worst-case request latency or guaranteed delivery.

followups.q: Should dropped logs be reported through the same overloaded logger?
followups.a: Avoid recursive overload reporting. Use a bounded, independent signal such as a counter or rate-limited fallback.

followups.q: Are in-memory queued audit events durable?
followups.a: No. A process crash can lose them; required audit guarantees need an appropriate durable delivery design.

questions.trap: Assuming asynchronous means nonblocking and lossless under every overload condition.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. No particular logging library's default policy is claimed. Round, level and frequency are estimates.

questions.question: Why can a parallel stream reduction return a different answer when its identity or combining operation is wrong?
questions.answer: A parallel reduction divides the input, accumulates partial results and combines them. Its identity must be neutral for the operation, and the combination must be associative so regrouping does not change the intended result. For addition, using a nonzero starting value as the identity can add that value once per partial reduction instead of once for the whole stream. Subtraction is not an associative combining operation. In a three-argument reduction, the accumulator and combiner must also be compatible. Mutable accumulation belongs in a properly designed collector rather than a shared mutable reduce identity. Floating-point addition adds another caveat: regrouping can change rounding, so exact reproducibility needs an explicit numeric strategy, not just a parallelism setting.

followups.q: Where should a one-time offset be added?
followups.a: Perform the reduction with its true neutral identity, then apply the offset once to the completed result.

followups.q: Does an ordered stream make subtraction safe in reduce?
followups.a: No. Encounter order does not remove the reduction's associativity requirement when partial results are grouped and combined.

questions.trap: Testing only a sequential stream and assuming the same accumulator is valid for parallel regrouping.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. GAP follows the supplied Stream API gap. This tests reduction algebra rather than external side effects in 034.

questions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap coordinate updates without locking the whole map?
questions.answer: In Java 21's common OpenJDK implementation, ConcurrentHashMap combines volatile table access and compare-and-set for some empty-bin insertions with synchronization scoped to a populated bin for other updates. Resizing coordinates participating threads rather than placing one application-wide lock around every operation. This allows unrelated bins to make progress independently, but collisions and mapping callbacks can still create contention. The Java API promises thread-safe operations, not this exact internal layout or a stable lock strategy, so I would state the JDK assumption explicitly. For an interview, I would connect the mechanism to the guarantee: individual map operations are coordinated, while a sequence such as get-then-put is not automatically atomic.

followups.q: Does ConcurrentHashMap lock the entire table for each put?
followups.a: No. The implementation coordinates updates more locally, though resizing and contention can involve multiple workers.

followups.q: Is get followed by put one atomic action?
followups.a: No. Use an atomic map operation such as putIfAbsent or compute when that is the needed contract.

questions.trap: Repeating Java 7 segment-array internals as the Java 21 implementation, or treating current internals as API guarantees.
verify: [VERIFY: recheck implementation details against the exact OpenJDK 21 update if an implementation-level answer is required]
questions.notes: Explicit CHM-internals readiness GAP; implementation summary is scoped to common OpenJDK 21, not the API contract.

questions.question: What does computeIfAbsent guarantee, and what should its mapping function avoid?
questions.answer: computeIfAbsent combines a missing-value check and insertion into one map operation, so callers do not need an unsafe get-then-put sequence. For ConcurrentHashMap, the mapping function should be short and simple and must not attempt to update other mappings of the same map; recursive updates can be detected and rejected. A slow callback can delay competing updates in the relevant coordination area, so network calls, database access and unrelated blocking work do not belong inside it. If loading can take time, store a deliberately managed future or use a separate single-flight mechanism with clear failure and eviction behavior. The map operation protects the association, not the full lifecycle of the loaded resource.

followups.q: Can the mapping function return null?
followups.a: Yes, but then no mapping is recorded and a later call can attempt the computation again.

followups.q: Should it perform a remote token refresh?
followups.a: Usually not directly; use an explicit in-flight coordination design with timeout and failure semantics.

questions.trap: Assuming computeIfAbsent makes an arbitrary long-running loader callback harmless or recursively reentrant.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; differs from the table-coordination mechanism in 076.

questions.question: Why must iteration over Collections.synchronizedMap be synchronized externally?
questions.answer: Collections.synchronizedMap wraps individual map operations with a common monitor, but iteration is a sequence of iterator calls rather than one map operation. Another thread can mutate the backing map between those calls unless the caller holds the wrapper's monitor for the entire traversal. The wrapper's documentation requires synchronizing on the returned map while iterating its views. The lock must be the wrapper object, not an unrelated lock or the raw backing map. Holding it for a long traversal can block writers, so if concurrent reads and writes are required, choose a collection with semantics that fit that access pattern instead of assuming the wrapper makes every compound action atomic.

followups.q: Does calling size and then iterating form one atomic snapshot?
followups.a: No. Those are separate operations unless one lock is held across the whole protocol.

followups.q: Which object should the traversal synchronize on?
followups.a: The synchronized wrapper returned by the factory, as specified by its API documentation.

questions.trap: Assuming synchronized individual methods automatically make an iterator traversal atomic.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; this concerns wrapper iteration, not ConcurrentHashMap traversal.

questions.question: Why can upgrading a read lock to a write lock deadlock with ReentrantReadWriteLock?
questions.answer: A write lock must exclude all readers, including the current thread's read hold. If a thread keeps its read lock while waiting to acquire the write lock, it contributes to the very condition that prevents the writer from proceeding. Another reader can do the same, leaving both waiting indefinitely. ReentrantReadWriteLock supports downgrading by acquiring the read lock while holding the write lock and then releasing write, but it does not provide a general atomic read-to-write upgrade. I would release the read lock, acquire write, and recheck the condition because state may have changed in the gap, or choose a different coordination design if that recheck is unacceptable.

followups.q: Is write-to-read downgrade supported?
followups.a: Yes, acquire read while holding write, then release write; the read hold remains.

followups.q: What correctness step follows releasing read before taking write?
followups.a: Revalidate the condition under write because another thread may have changed the state.

questions.trap: Claiming a read holder can simply block for write while retaining its read lock.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; distinct from selecting a read-write lock in 012.

questions.question: What constraints matter when converting or composing StampedLock modes?
questions.answer: StampedLock is not reentrant: a thread cannot treat it like ReentrantLock and reacquire a mode it already holds. Each successful acquisition returns a stamp that must be used for the matching unlock or validation. Conversion methods attempt a mode change without first releasing protection, but conversion can fail and return zero; code must then follow a deliberate fallback rather than assume ownership changed. Holding a read stamp while blocking for a write stamp can still prevent progress. I would keep the protected region small, track each stamp explicitly and prefer a simpler lock when reentrancy or condition variables are needed. Optimistic reads remain provisional until validated, as covered separately.

followups.q: Does a failed tryConvertToWriteLock release the read lock?
followups.a: No; a failed conversion does not grant write ownership, so follow the documented fallback for the held mode.

followups.q: Can StampedLock support Condition.await?
followups.a: No. It does not implement the condition-wait contract provided by ReentrantLock.

questions.trap: Using StampedLock as though it were reentrant or assuming a conversion always succeeds.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; does not repeat the optimistic field-read scenario in 066.

questions.question: Does choosing a fair lock guarantee that every waiting thread runs next?
questions.answer: A fair ReentrantLock favors the longest-waiting contender when lock acquisition is contended, reducing barging, but it does not control operating-system scheduling or guarantee a thread will execute immediately. Fairness can reduce throughput because a newly ready thread cannot exploit a temporarily free lock ahead of queued waiters. Untimed tryLock can also barge even when the lock is configured fair. I would enable fairness only when starvation risk or latency distribution justifies the throughput trade-off, and verify behavior under the real workload. Fair locking is a queue policy, not a global guarantee about CPU time or completion order.

followups.q: Does fairness ensure FIFO completion?
followups.a: No. It influences lock acquisition under contention, not scheduling after a thread acquires it.

followups.q: Can untimed tryLock respect the fairness setting?
followups.a: The untimed tryLock may barge; consult the method contract rather than infer from constructor fairness.

questions.trap: Promising strict FIFO execution or assuming fairness is always safer and faster.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; method-specific fairness semantics matter.

questions.question: What does monitor pinning mean for virtual threads on Java 21?
questions.answer: Pinning means a virtual thread cannot unmount from its carrier during a blocking operation, so that carrier remains occupied. Under Java 21's JEP 444 behavior, blocking while executing synchronized code can pin a virtual thread; certain native or foreign calls can also prevent unmounting. A short synchronized section is not automatically a problem, but frequent long blocking operations while holding a monitor can reduce carrier availability. Diagnose with supported virtual-thread events or tracing on the exact JDK before rewriting synchronization. This is explicitly a Java 21 statement: JDK 24 changed monitor pinning behavior, so an answer about a later runtime must be checked against that release rather than copied forward.

followups.q: Does every synchronized block pin a virtual thread?
followups.a: The concern is blocking while pinned; ordinary short monitor use is not the same as a long blocking operation.

followups.q: Can Java 21 pinning guidance be applied unchanged to Java 24?
followups.a: No. JDK 24 changed monitor pinning; verify the target release's behavior.

questions.trap: Claiming synchronized always pins every virtual thread on every JDK, or claiming Java 21 never pins on monitors.
verify: [VERIFY: check the target vendor's JEP 444/JEP 491 implementation and virtual-thread diagnostics; Java 21 baseline stated, no web verification performed]
questions.notes: Java 21 behavior is stated as the known baseline; later-release details remain explicitly unverified.

questions.question: How does ScopedValue differ from ThreadLocal in the Java 21 preview?
questions.answer: In Java 21, ScopedValue was a preview API for binding a value to a bounded dynamic scope. Code in that scope can read the binding, while callers cannot arbitrarily replace it the way they can mutate a ThreadLocal value. The API was preview, so compiling or running code against it required preview features to be enabled, and its shape was not a final cross-release contract. This can make request context easier to reason about across structured calls, but do not assume automatic propagation into every executor task. ThreadLocal remains mutable thread-associated state and still needs cleanup on reused workers. I would state the JDK version and verify the target release before choosing either mechanism.

followups.q: Was ScopedValue final in Java 21?
followups.a: No. It was a preview feature in Java 21 and required preview enablement.

followups.q: Does a ScopedValue automatically follow work submitted to any executor?
followups.a: Do not assume that; propagation depends on the structured API and execution boundary.

questions.trap: Presenting the Java 21 preview as a final API or as a drop-in mutable ThreadLocal replacement.
verify: [VERIFY: confirm preview/final status and API behavior in the exact target JDK release notes; Java 21 baseline stated without web verification]
questions.notes: Known Java 21 preview status is explicit; no claim is made about later finalization.

questions.question: What problem does StructuredTaskScope address, and what was its Java 21 status?
questions.answer: Structured concurrency groups related child tasks under a lexical scope so their lifetime, joining and failure handling are visible at the parent operation. The parent can wait for subtasks, apply a policy such as fail-fast or collect results, and avoid orphaned work outliving the request. In Java 21, StructuredTaskScope was a preview API, not a finalized standard library contract; preview enablement and release-specific API changes matter. It does not make arbitrary blocking calls cancellable or define an application's partial-result policy for it. I would explain the lifecycle benefit, then verify the exact preview API and cancellation behavior for the JDK being used before writing code against it.

followups.q: Was StructuredTaskScope final in Java 21?
followups.a: No. It was a preview API and required preview enablement.

followups.q: Does cancelling a scope forcibly stop uncooperative work?
followups.a: No. Cancellation is cooperative and depends on tasks responding to interruption or cancellation.

questions.trap: Describing StructuredTaskScope as a final Java 21 API or as guaranteed forced cancellation.
verify: [VERIFY: confirm StructuredTaskScope preview status, API shape and shutdown semantics for the target release; Java 21 baseline stated without web verification]
questions.notes: Java 21 preview assumption is explicit; current release status was not researched online.

questions.question: Where do no-executor CompletableFuture async stages run, and why can that matter?
questions.answer: For ordinary CompletableFuture instances, async methods without an explicit executor generally use the common pool's default asynchronous execution facility. Non-async continuations may instead run on the thread that completes the prior stage or attaches the continuation when the prior stage is already complete. A blocking callback can therefore occupy a shared worker or caller thread unexpectedly. I would pass a bounded, purpose-appropriate executor for blocking downstream calls and keep inline continuations short. The exact executor behavior can differ for custom CompletionStage implementations, so I would not assume every implementation follows CompletableFuture defaults. Thread placement is a capacity and latency decision, not merely a stylistic choice.

followups.q: Does thenApplyAsync always use the common pool?
followups.a: Without an explicit executor, ordinary CompletableFuture uses its default async facility; a custom implementation can differ.

followups.q: Can thenApply run on the request thread?
followups.a: Yes, depending on completion timing and implementation; keep non-async callbacks short.

questions.trap: Assuming every continuation runs on the executor passed to the original supplyAsync call.
questions.notes: Distinct from 059, which asks whether the original custom executor is inherited.

questions.question: What is the difference between orTimeout and completeOnTimeout?
questions.answer: Both methods arrange a timeout completion for the CompletableFuture on which they are invoked, and both return that same future rather than a separate timeout view. orTimeout completes it exceptionally with TimeoutException if it has not already completed; completeOnTimeout completes it normally with the supplied fallback value. Neither method by itself guarantees that the underlying I/O or computation is cancelled. If the future represents a client request, I need a separate cancellation or deadline mechanism understood by that client. I would choose fallback only when it is semantically valid, and ensure late completion cannot trigger duplicate side effects after the caller has timed out.

followups.q: Does orTimeout cancel the supplier thread?
followups.a: No. Timeout completion does not itself guarantee interruption or cancellation of the computation.

followups.q: When is completeOnTimeout safe?
followups.a: Only when the fallback is a valid business result and late work has controlled side effects.

questions.trap: Treating a timed-out future as proof that the downstream operation has stopped.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; distinct from timeout-budget accounting in 054.

questions.question: When would you use exceptionally, handle or whenComplete in a future chain?
questions.answer: exceptionally is a recovery stage: it receives a failure and can provide a replacement value, while a successful upstream value passes through. handle sees either success or failure and returns a new value, so it is useful when both outcomes need one transformation. whenComplete is intended for observation and normally preserves the upstream outcome, although an exception thrown by the callback can affect its dependent stage. All return dependent stages, so ignoring the returned stage can hide a callback failure. I would keep recovery policy separate from metrics or logging, unwrap causes where needed, and make sure fallback values do not turn an unavailable downstream into false business success.

followups.q: Which one can transform either outcome into a value?
followups.a: handle receives both the value and failure and returns a dependent result.

followups.q: Does whenComplete guarantee its callback cannot affect the returned stage?
followups.a: No. A callback exception can make the dependent stage exceptional.

questions.trap: Using a fallback stage that silently converts every infrastructure failure into valid business data.
questions.notes: Complements 058's callback-failure edge case without duplicating it.

questions.question: What happens to later executions when a periodic scheduled task throws?
questions.answer: For ScheduledExecutorService periodic tasks, an execution that terminates exceptionally suppresses subsequent executions of that periodic task. The scheduler does not repeatedly invoke a failing job as though nothing happened. This can look like a scheduler that silently stopped, especially if the returned ScheduledFuture is ignored. I would retain the future or instrument the task boundary, report the exception, and decide whether a particular failure should be retried with explicit backoff. Catching every Throwable and continuing can hide VM-level failures, so catch expected operational exceptions and preserve a visible failure policy. This differs from a one-shot task, whose exception is observed through its Future or executor policy.

followups.q: Will scheduleAtFixedRate run again after an uncaught exception?
followups.a: No. An exceptional execution suppresses later executions of that periodic task.

followups.q: Should the task catch Throwable and ignore it?
followups.a: No. Handle expected failures deliberately and make fatal or unexpected failures observable.

questions.trap: Assuming the scheduler logs every task failure and automatically retries the next period.
questions.notes: General ScheduledExecutorService contract; exact logging depends on how the returned future is observed.

questions.question: Why can cancelled delayed tasks remain in a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor queue?
questions.answer: A cancelled delayed task may remain in the scheduler's delay queue until its delay expires, depending on the executor policy. The future can report cancellation while its queue node and captured task state remain retained. A workload that repeatedly schedules long delays and cancels early can therefore accumulate queue entries. ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor exposes remove-on-cancel policy to remove cancelled tasks promptly; enable it when that retention pattern matters and verify the target JDK configuration. I would also inspect task captures and schedule volume rather than assume cancellation immediately frees every referenced object. Queue cleanup has a cost, so choose policy based on workload evidence.

followups.q: Does Future.cancel always remove its queue node immediately?
followups.a: Not by default in every scheduler policy; check ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor's remove-on-cancel setting.

followups.q: What else can a cancelled task retain?
followups.a: Its callable or runnable can retain request data, clients or other object graphs until queue removal.

questions.trap: Equating cancelled future state with immediate release of every queued task reference.
questions.notes: Specific ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor policy detail; complements general cancelled-backlog question 062.

questions.question: What does ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker provide when a worker must block?
questions.answer: ForkJoinPool is optimized for tasks that split into smaller tasks and frequently help execute other work. A worker blocked on an external condition can reduce available parallelism. ManagedBlocker lets code describe whether a blocking action is releasable and perform that action, giving the pool an opportunity to compensate with another worker when possible. It is not a guarantee of unlimited replacement threads or a cure for arbitrary blocking dependencies. I would prefer keeping blocking I/O outside CPU-oriented fork-join work, use a dedicated executor when appropriate, and use ManagedBlocker only when its contract matches the operation and the pool can safely compensate.

followups.q: Does ManagedBlocker guarantee another worker is created?
followups.a: No. It allows the pool to compensate when possible; resource limits and policy still apply.

followups.q: Should all HTTP calls use the common fork-join pool?
followups.a: No. Isolate blocking work or use an I/O-appropriate execution strategy.

questions.trap: Presenting managed blocking as a guarantee that blocking tasks cannot starve a pool.
questions.notes: Specific mechanism complements the broader common-pool risk in 022; readiness remains untested.

questions.question: How do LockSupport.park and unpark differ from a one-time notification?
questions.answer: LockSupport gives each thread a permit with at most one accumulated unit. unpark makes a permit available, including when called before the thread parks, so the signal is not simply lost in that ordering. Repeated unparks do not accumulate an unbounded count. park can also return spuriously or because the thread is interrupted, so callers must loop on a condition whose state is protected by a synchronization protocol. Unlike Object.wait, park does not require owning a monitor and does not release one. Higher-level synchronizers build queueing and memory-order rules around these primitives; application code should usually use those abstractions instead of inventing its own protocol.

followups.q: Can unpark before park be remembered?
followups.a: Yes, one permit can be available for a subsequent park by that thread.

followups.q: Does park release a synchronized monitor?
followups.a: No. It is not a replacement for Object.wait's monitor-release behavior.

questions.trap: Treating park as a counting semaphore or assuming every park returns only after an unpark.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; application code should prefer established synchronizers.

questions.question: How do VarHandle plain, opaque, acquire/release and volatile accesses differ conceptually?
questions.answer: VarHandle exposes variable access with explicit ordering modes. Plain access follows ordinary field rules; opaque access provides coherent access to that location without the broader ordering of acquire/release. A release write orders earlier actions before publication, and a matching acquire read orders later actions after observing it. Volatile access provides the stronger volatile ordering and visibility contract. These modes are low-level tools: choosing a weaker mode requires a complete proof for the data structure, not a performance guess. I would prefer volatile, atomics or locks unless a measured implementation needs a VarHandle and has tests for the intended publication protocol.

followups.q: What ordering does a release write provide?
followups.a: It orders preceding actions before the release for a matching observing acquire protocol.

followups.q: Should opaque replace volatile by default?
followups.a: No. Weaker ordering is correct only when the full protocol proves it sufficient.

questions.trap: Treating memory modes as interchangeable performance levels without specifying the synchronization protocol.
verify: [VERIFY: consult the exact Java 21 VarHandle access-mode specification before relying on subtle ordering claims]
questions.notes: Conceptual summary; no custom lock-free algorithm or benchmark is claimed.

questions.question: Why must an AtomicReference update function be safe to run more than once?
questions.answer: Methods such as updateAndGet may implement an update as a compare-and-set retry loop. If another thread changes the reference after the function reads the old value, the function can be evaluated again with a newer value. Therefore the function should be side-effect-free: logging a payment, sending a message or incrementing an unrelated counter inside it can happen multiple times even though one reference update succeeds. Compute a new immutable state from the supplied prior state, then perform external effects after a successful transition using an idempotent protocol. Atomicity applies to the reference update, not to arbitrary side effects executed by the callback.

followups.q: Can the update function run once exactly?
followups.a: Do not assume that; contention can cause reevaluation.

followups.q: How do you combine an atomic transition with a message send?
followups.a: Use an explicit outbox or idempotent coordination strategy rather than sending inside a retryable function.

questions.trap: Putting a non-idempotent side effect inside a CAS-based update lambda.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; focuses on callback retry semantics, not the ABA example in 005.

questions.question: What is false sharing, and when is padding a reasonable response?
questions.answer: False sharing occurs when independent variables updated by different cores occupy the same cache-coherence line. The threads do not share a logical field, but writes cause the hardware to transfer ownership of that line, creating coherence traffic and poor throughput. It is a hardware and memory-layout effect, not a Java data race. I would suspect it only after profiling a hot, highly contended structure and confirming scaling stalls; then compare a measured layout or a striped accumulator. Manual padding and internal annotations can be nonportable or increase footprint, so do not add them from a source-level guess. LongAdder is one higher-level option for heavily contended statistics.

followups.q: Is false sharing a correctness race?
followups.a: Not by itself; it is a performance interaction from cache-line ownership.

followups.q: Would you pad every frequently written field?
followups.a: No. Measure first because padding can increase memory use and layout assumptions are platform-dependent.

questions.trap: Treating false sharing as two threads writing the same Java variable or as a guaranteed diagnosis from low throughput.
questions.notes: Hardware-level concept; no portable cache-line size is asserted.

questions.question: What is the difference between obstruction-free, lock-free and wait-free progress?
questions.answer: These terms describe system progress guarantees, not simply whether code uses a mutex. Obstruction-free means an operation can complete if it eventually runs alone without interference. Lock-free means the system as a whole continues completing operations under contention, though one particular thread may starve. Wait-free is stronger: every operation completes in a bounded number of its own steps. A CAS loop may be lock-free while repeatedly losing threads are delayed indefinitely; it is not automatically wait-free. I would state which progress property an algorithm proves and separately discuss fairness, latency and resource bounds. For ordinary application code, a well-chosen lock can be easier to reason about and meet the real service objective.

followups.q: Does lock-free mean every thread finishes?
followups.a: No. It promises system-wide progress, not bounded progress for each individual thread.

followups.q: Is a lock-free algorithm always faster?
followups.a: No. Contention, retries and hardware determine performance; measure equivalent semantics.

questions.trap: Using lock-free as a synonym for wait-free, fair or universally faster.
questions.notes: Definitions are algorithmic progress guarantees, not readiness claims.

questions.question: Why should code avoid synchronizing on value-based objects such as boxed values?
questions.answer: A synchronized block coordinates through the identity of its monitor object, but value-based objects are intended to be treated as values rather than identity-bearing locks. Boxed values may be shared through caching, so two unrelated code paths can unexpectedly synchronize on the same instance. Some value-based classes document synchronization as unsupported or warn that behavior may change. Use a private final lock object with a clear owner instead. That gives the critical section a stable identity and avoids depending on boxing, interning or implementation-specific object reuse. Do not synchronize on a public argument or string literal either, because unrelated callers can acquire that same monitor.

followups.q: Why can synchronizing on Integer.valueOf be surprising?
followups.a: Boxing caches can make equal values share an object identity across otherwise unrelated code.

followups.q: What is a safer lock target?
followups.a: A private final object dedicated to protecting the invariant.

questions.trap: Assuming equal-looking boxed values always produce distinct monitor identities.
verify: [VERIFY: check the value-based-class synchronization warning for each specific Java 21 class/API]
questions.notes: No assertion that every wrapper value is cached; behavior depends on API and value.

questions.question: What happens if a CyclicBarrier action fails or one participant times out?
questions.answer: A CyclicBarrier releases its parties when the required number arrive, and one designated barrier action can run before they are released. If a party is interrupted, times out or fails while waiting, the barrier becomes broken for that generation and waiting parties receive BrokenBarrierException; a failing barrier action also breaks the barrier. Callers need an explicit recovery policy, such as abandoning that batch or resetting only after all participants have left the old generation. Resetting is not a substitute for understanding which workers still hold old work. This differs from a CountDownLatch, which is one-shot and does not have reusable generations.

followups.q: Does CyclicBarrier automatically recover after one participant times out?
followups.a: The generation is broken; participants must handle that outcome or coordinate a reset.

followups.q: Can a barrier action safely perform arbitrary blocking I/O?
followups.a: It delays release of the waiting parties, so keep it bounded and define failure behavior.

questions.trap: Treating reset as proof that every participant from the failed generation has stopped.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; complements synchronizer selection in 025.

questions.question: What is the correct predicate protocol when using a ReentrantLock Condition?
questions.answer: A Condition signal is a prompt to recheck shared state, not the state change itself. The thread checks its predicate while holding the associated lock, calls await in a while loop if the predicate is false, and await atomically releases that lock while waiting and reacquires it before returning. A producer changes the predicate under the same lock and signals the appropriate condition. Signal does not release the lock immediately, and a wake can be spurious or another waiter may consume the condition first. I would use separate Conditions for distinct queues such as not-empty and not-full, while keeping each predicate and its lock ownership explicit.

followups.q: Does signal transfer the lock to a waiter?
followups.a: No. The signaller keeps the lock until it releases it; the waiter then competes to reacquire.

followups.q: Why use while instead of if around await?
followups.a: Wakeups can be spurious and the predicate may no longer hold when the thread reacquires the lock.

questions.trap: Treating signal as a stored event or as proof that the awaited predicate is true.
questions.notes: Condition-based protocol is distinct from intrinsic-monitor details in 007.

questions.question: How does ExecutorCompletionService help when task results should be handled in completion order?
questions.answer: ExecutorCompletionService wraps an executor and places completed task futures on a completion queue. A consumer can take the next finished future rather than block first on the slowest task submitted earliest, then call get to obtain the value or observe failure. This is useful for independent fan-out work when results can be processed as they arrive. The completion queue does not impose a business ordering, bound all submitted work automatically, or decide how partial failures affect the response. I would bound task admission separately, handle cancellation and exceptions, and preserve request identity when aggregating outcomes. If output order matters, collect results with their original index and reorder explicitly.

followups.q: Does completion order equal submission order?
followups.a: No. It reflects which tasks complete first.

followups.q: Does the service decide all-or-nothing behavior?
followups.a: No. The caller still defines the policy for failed or missing task outcomes.

questions.trap: Assuming completion-order consumption also bounds task submission or preserves original result order.
questions.notes: Builds on completion-order question 037 with the concrete JDK abstraction and its limits.

questions.question: Does a fair Semaphore prevent barging when callers use tryAcquire()?
questions.answer: Semaphore fairness orders blocking acquisitions approximately by arrival at its internal queue when permits become available, but the untimed tryAcquire method may take a permit immediately even when other threads are queued. That barging behavior is documented and can surprise code that uses tryAcquire as a nonblocking fairness-preserving check. Timed tryAcquire with a zero timeout has different fairness semantics from the untimed form. I would choose fairness for starvation behavior only after checking the exact method contract, and I would still bound downstream concurrency and observe wait-time distribution.
