Fairness does not guarantee prompt CPU scheduling after a permit is granted.

followups.q: Does untimed tryAcquire honor a fair semaphore queue?
followups.a: It may barge and acquire an available permit ahead of queued threads.

followups.q: Does fairness guarantee a permit holder runs immediately?
followups.a: No. It affects permit acquisition ordering, not operating-system scheduling.

questions.trap: Assuming a fair constructor makes every acquisition method strictly FIFO.
questions.notes: Method-specific fairness contract; distinct from permit ownership and release in 041.

questions.question: How does ForkJoinPool differ from ThreadPoolExecutor?
questions.answer: A ThreadPoolExecutor has one shared work queue that its threads pull from; it suits independent, coarse-grained tasks such as requests and jobs, and blocking I/O is acceptable if the pool is sized for it. A ForkJoinPool gives each worker its own deque and lets idle workers steal tasks from the tail of other workers' deques, which suits recursive divide-and-conquer work expressed as RecursiveTask or RecursiveAction. Its workers should not block, because blocking removes parallelism and can starve the pool. The common pool also backs parallel streams and default CompletableFuture async stages, so blocking work there affects the whole JVM.

followups.q: What does work stealing improve?
followups.a: Load balance when tasks split unevenly, because idle workers take queued subtasks from busy ones.

followups.q: Where can a ForkJoinPool worker still block safely?
followups.a: Only through ManagedBlocker, which lets the pool add compensating threads.

questions.trap: Describing ForkJoinPool as simply a faster thread pool. Its design assumes small, non-blocking, divisible tasks.

questions.question: How do you make a class and its methods thread-safe?
questions.answer: Prefer designs with nothing to protect. Immutable objects need no synchronization. Confinement keeps state local to one thread through method locals or ThreadLocal. Where state must be shared, guard each piece with one consistent lock, using synchronized or ReentrantLock over the smallest critical section; volatile gives visibility for a single flag but not atomicity for compound actions such as i++. Atomic classes and concurrent collections replace hand-rolled locking for counters and maps. Publish objects safely, avoid leaking this from constructors, and make fields final where possible. In Spring, singleton beans should be stateless.

followups.q: Does volatile make count++ safe?
followups.a: No. It is a read, an increment and a write; use an atomic class or a lock.

followups.q: Why must the same lock guard every access to a piece of state?
followups.a: Different locks do not exclude each other, so mutual exclusion is lost.

questions.trap: Adding synchronized to every method and calling the class thread-safe; compound actions across calls can still race.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.6 (Accolite, Randstad). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S05-051, JH-S05-003.

questions.question: How should you size and design threading for CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work?
questions.answer: CPU-bound tasks keep a core busy, so the pool size should be about the number of cores; more threads add context-switching cost without more throughput. I/O-bound tasks spend most of their time waiting on the network, disk or a database, so a pool can be much larger than the core count, up to the limits of downstream systems. A common estimate is threads of about cores times target utilisation times one plus wait time over service time. For high-concurrency blocking I/O on Java 21, virtual threads or an asynchronous design avoid dedicating an OS thread to every waiting call. Use separate pools per workload type so slow I/O cannot starve CPU work.

followups.q: Why not size an I/O pool at the core count?
followups.a: Threads blocked on I/O waste cores, so throughput is capped by the pool rather than the hardware.

followups.q: What limits an I/O pool from growing indefinitely?
followups.a: Downstream capacity such as database connections or rate limits, plus memory for thread stacks.

questions.trap: Applying one pool size to every workload. CPU-bound and I/O-bound tasks need different sizing.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.8 (Capgemini). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S05-024, JH-S05-050.

questions.question: How many threads can a JVM run on one machine, and what limits it?
questions.answer: The JVM sets no fixed number; the limits come from memory and the operating system. Each platform thread maps to an OS thread and reserves stack space (-Xss, commonly about 1 MB on 64-bit Linux), so a thousand threads reserve roughly a gigabyte of address space. OS limits such as the per-user process limit (ulimit -u), kernel thread maximums and memory mappings also apply. In practice a few thousand platform threads is a ceiling before scheduling overhead dominates. Virtual threads in Java 21 are lightweight and heap-allocated, so millions are feasible for I/O-bound work.

followups.q: How does the OS run more threads than cores?
followups.a: The scheduler time-slices runnable threads across cores and switches between them.

followups.q: Does a virtual thread need its own OS thread?
followups.a: No. It is mounted on a carrier thread only while running and is unmounted when it blocks.

questions.trap: Quoting a single magic number of threads. The honest answer is that memory and OS limits decide, and workload type matters more.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.9 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S04-005, JH-S05-024.

questions.question: Is Spring's @Async multithreaded or single-threaded, and how do you configure it?
questions.answer: @Async methods run on a TaskExecutor thread pool, not on the caller's request thread, so the work is multithreaded; only the reactive stack, such as WebFlux on Netty, is event-loop based. Enable it with @EnableAsync and define a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor-backed executor with core size, maximum size, queue capacity and a thread name prefix. Async works through a proxy, so self-invocation does not trigger it and the method must be public and called from another bean. Return void or CompletableFuture; exceptions in void methods need an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. Without a custom executor, Spring Boot's auto-configured one is used, so size an executor explicitly for production.

followups.q: Why does calling an @Async method from the same class run synchronously?
followups.a: The call bypasses the Spring proxy, so no asynchronous interception happens.

followups.q: Where do uncaught exceptions go for a void async method?
followups.a: To the configured AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, since no caller can receive them.

questions.trap: Calling @Async single-threaded or event-loop based. That describes the reactive stack, not annotation-driven async.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.12 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron), Concentrix). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S05-015, JH-S05-085.

questions.question: How do you call two REST services in parallel from one microservice and combine the results?
questions.answer: Start both calls as CompletableFuture instances on your own bounded executor, then combine them: CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join() waits for both, or a.thenCombine(b, Response::new) merges the results directly. Add orTimeout or completeOnTimeout and an exceptionally fallback so one slow dependency cannot hang the request. Avoid the default common pool for blocking HTTP calls. In WebFlux, Mono.zip(a, b) expresses the same idea reactively, and on Java 21 virtual threads let you write blocking code that still runs concurrently. Decide up front whether partial results are acceptable.

followups.q: What does allOf return?
followups.a: A CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when every input completes, so you read each input future yourself.

followups.q: What happens to the second call if the first fails?
followups.a: It keeps running unless you cancel it; CompletableFuture does not cancel siblings automatically.

questions.trap: Using the default common pool for blocking REST calls, so one slow service starves unrelated work.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.13 (Concentrix). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S05-019, JH-S05-038.

questions.question: You must send millions of notifications asynchronously: do you use Java threads or Kafka?
questions.answer: Use a durable broker such as Kafka for the bulk path. An in-process thread pool offers no durability, so a restart loses queued work; it has no real back-pressure, and a queue that grows without bound eventually exhausts memory; and it only scales within one JVM. Kafka provides durable buffering, replay, partition-level parallelism, consumer groups that scale by adding instances, ordering per key and a dead-letter topic for poison messages. Consumers need idempotent processing because delivery is at least once. Reserve in-JVM async for short, non-critical, fire-and-forget work.

followups.q: How do you scale the consumers?
followups.a: Add consumer instances to the group up to the partition count, and add partitions if you need more parallelism.

followups.q: How do you avoid duplicate sends on retries?
followups.a: Make the send idempotent, for example by keying on a notification id and deduplicating.

questions.trap: Answering with a bigger thread pool. A pool cannot give durability, replay or scale beyond one process.
